name: Koder
tagline: Online judge that runs untrusted code in isolated Docker containers.
description: A full-stack online judge for function-signature problems. Users submit JavaScript, Java, or Python; language-specific BullMQ workers grade each submission in a per-submission Docker sandbox and store the verdict.

caseStudy.problem: An online judge has to run code it cannot trust. Grading in the request path would block the API and let a malicious or runaway submission affect the server.
caseStudy.users: Signed-in users solving problems, and administrators who manage questions and contests.
caseStudy.contribution: Architecture, API, queue and worker design, sandbox hardening, and the grading pipeline. Source is on GitHub for review.
features: Function-signature problems with JavaScript, Java, and Python submissions
Cookie-authenticated REST API under /api/v1, plus admin routes protected by an admin-role check
One BullMQ queue and worker per language (js-queue, java-queue, python-queue)
Sample and hidden test cases graded in batches of up to 50
Contests and leaderboards, and an admin interface for questions and contests
Shared @koder/shared workspace package for models, queue config, verdicts, and runner generation

architecture.summary: Three kinds of process: a Next.js frontend, an Express API, and one worker per language. Redis carries jobs; MongoDB stores submissions and questions. Docker Compose supplies MongoDB and Redis for local development only.
steps: The frontend posts { language, code } to POST /api/v1/submissions/:questionId.
The API validates the language, saves a submission as pending, and enqueues an execute job on the matching queue.
The language worker loads the submission and question, generates the runner, and starts one Docker container.
Test cases stream to the runner over a line-based Base64 protocol; Java is compiled with javac first.
The worker records the first failure, or Accepted, in MongoDB and force-removes the container.
The frontend picks up the result through an events stream, falling back to polling GET /api/v1/submissions/:submissionId.

decisions.title: Queue between API and grading
decisions.body: Submission handling returns immediately after enqueueing, so slow or hostile code never occupies an API request.

decisions.title: One container per submission
decisions.body: The worker streams a batch of test cases to a single runner process instead of starting a container for every test case.

decisions.title: Namespaced sandbox directories
decisions.body: BullMQ job IDs repeat across queues, so sandbox paths use language plus job ID (for example python-1) and are checked to stay under the worker temp directory.

decisions.title: Fail-fast judging
decisions.body: Execution stops at the first failing test case and records that verdict.

challenges.solution: Containers run with no network, all capabilities dropped, no-new-privileges, a non-root user, a read-only root filesystem, a 64 MB tmpfs, and 256 MB memory, 1 CPU, and 64 process limits.
Watchdogs cap each test case at 2 seconds and the whole submission at 45 seconds; timed-out processes are killed and the container removed.

challenges.challenge: Same job ID in different queues
challenges.solution: Sandbox directories are keyed by language and job ID, with path validation, after a collision was found and fixed.

testing: CI-safe Node test suites for backend and workers using built-in assert (npm test)
A Docker-based sandbox collision test exists but is run manually
outcomes: ISSUES.md in the repository records ISSUE-001 through ISSUE-015 as complete, including sandbox hardening and Python support
limitations: Docker enforces the memory cap, but out-of-memory failures surface as runtime errors rather than a Memory Limit Exceeded verdict
Redis fixed-window rate limiting is implemented on auth routes (10 req/min) and submissions (20 req/min), but automated account lockout after repeated failed attempts is not implemented
No CI workflow in the repository, and no deployed demo
Worker capacity values are host-specific and not benchmarked for production

name: Tasky
tagline: AI assistant that turns Gmail, Calendar, and Tasks into a single task dashboard.
description: A Next.js app that connects a user's Google Calendar and Google Tasks, reads Gmail, and uses OpenAI gpt-4o-mini agents to turn emails and natural-language instructions into structured tasks and events.

caseStudy.problem: Deadlines and requests are scattered across email, calendar, and task lists, so turning them into actionable items is manual work.
caseStudy.contribution: Full-stack implementation: Google API integration, the agent modules, authentication, and the dashboard.
features: Unified dashboard for Google Calendar events and Google Tasks
Separate agent modules for tasks, email, calendar, and prompt-guided JSON instruction interpretation using gpt-4o-mini
Clerk authentication with Google OAuth 2.0 access
Mongoose models for user storage in MongoDB
limitations: No live demo or usage numbers are published
Structured outputs rely on prompt-engineered JSON format instructions parsed via JSON.parse rather than OpenAI's native tools/function-calling or JSON schema response_format APIs
